newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition drops budget freeze idea for now.
newsitem.headline: German coalition drops budget freeze idea for now.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition decided on Tuesday not to impose a freeze on extra state spending which would help contain the budget deficit so that Bonn can meet its goal of qualifying for European monetary union (EMU).

Joachim Hoerster, chief parliamentary whip of the alliance of Christian Democrats and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), said a freeze had been discussed at length by coalition leaders but would not be imposed "for the time being".

Speculation has been mounting that Finance Minister Theo Waigel would choke off extra outgoings since the government last month revised up its forecast of the 1997 German budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product.
The Maastricht treaty, which Germany wants to be strictly interpreted, sets a three percent deficit ceiling this year for countries wanting to join the launch of the euro in 1999.

Waigel had been keeping his options open, but with budgeted cuts in spending blamed in part for pushing unemployment in January up to 4.7 million, the highest since 1933, the coalition appears reluctant to tighten the screw any further.

The coalition did, however, agree to cut back state spending on consumption and divert more funds to job-creating investment. That, Hoerster said, means the government will be seeking ways to reduce spending on social security benefits.
